text: Lesson 10 introduced both encodings individually. This lesson puts them side by side on the same concrete example, so you can see exactly where qubit cost, circuit cost, and practical trade-offs diverge.

Take a dataset with four continuous features: 1.0, 0.4, 1.2, and 0.8 radians. Angle encoding needs 4 qubits, one rotation each. Amplitude encoding needs only 2 qubits, since 4 values fit into 4 amplitudes. Normalizing the vector: its norm is the square root of 3.24, equal to 1.8, giving a normalized vector of about 0.556, 0.222, 0.667, 0.444. Same four numbers, four qubits versus two — and that compression advantage grows as feature count grows.

But the qubit savings aren't free. Angle encoding's circuit is shallow: one single-qubit rotation per feature, applied in parallel, constant depth regardless of feature count. Amplitude encoding, preparing an arbitrary state, can need up to on the order of 2 to the n gates in the worst case. On NISQ hardware, each of those extra gates is extra noise exposure, which can partly or fully offset the qubit-count win.

The encoding choice also shapes what a quantum kernel measures. Under angle encoding with a single-qubit RY feature map, the kernel works out exactly to cosine squared of x minus x prime over 2 — for x equals 0.4 and x prime equals 1.2, that's cosine squared of negative 0.4, about 0.8484. Amplitude encoding's kernel, by contrast, is the squared overlap of the raw normalized vectors, essentially a quantum cosine similarity. These are genuinely different similarity measures, not just different implementations of the same idea.

Next lesson assembles everything from this chapter into one named architecture: the variational quantum classifier, combining encoding, ansatz, measurement, and loss into a complete, working pipeline.
